basis: Ushojo picelo smooth matches the picchila/picchala slippery adjective set, with final o and medial stress. The medial e favors no uniquely determined old a/i formation, so8152 remains an alternative; do not select picchilá merely to obtain old oxytony.

Brokskat zon and Ushojo jon snake match jantú through nt simplification and palatal/sibilant onset, with the specifically attested creature-to-snake semantic narrowing. Both tokens are short unmarked monosyllables.

Ushojo him snow retains the m of himá, independently distinguishing it from hin forms whose old source may be śīna/snih/himna. No accent is marked, so this supplies segmental ancestry but not an accent outcome.

Ushojo kamalo soft matches kōmalá with final o and medial root-final stress, despite no long vowel being transcribed. It supports a morphological syllable-position correspondence independently of Palula's long medial aa.

Ushojo kacak some is the same quantity-interrogative base as kacaak how many, showing interrogative-to-indefinite use and the same final stress. The transcribed length difference is retained and may reflect context rather than separate ancestry.
Ushojo puc son matches putrá through tr affrication and final vowel loss. It is a short unmarked monosyllable and therefore gives no early/late contrast.

Brokskat ẓamoo son-in-law matches jā́mātṛ with a reduced kinship formation and final oo stress. The final vowel/kinship suffix and possible regional borrowing must be examined; the old initial accent is not transparently preserved.
Ushojo nuṣ son's wife matches snuṣā́ after initial s loss and final vowel loss, independently distinct from vadhū bride forms. No accent is marked on the resulting short monosyllable.
Brokskat cukro sour preserves the cukra consonant cluster and final o adjective ending, with initial stress. It is a root-stressed adjective reflex of old cukrá, not a śukta lexical replacement.

Ushojo ṛaz speak matches the regional ra/raz speaking root also seen in Brokskat raazis, with the same ultimate rápati versus rásati uncertainty. It is a root-family link only and has no marked accent.

Ushojo jola spider matches jāla net/web through agent/object semantic transfer, with final stress. The modern creature noun may be a derivative or truncated compound; it cannot be counted as direct preservation of the simple jā́la net noun's initial accent.

Brokskat ortsu spring of water is a plausible útsa descendant with an r extension/metathesis compared with regional uts. Initial stress is explicit, but the added r and final u require verification, so retain a provisional relation rather than a strict direct-reflex claim.

Brokskat uthis stand contains ut plus sthā standing root and recurring citation is morphology, matching Palula uthii. Final stress belongs to the modern verb formation; the old perfective utsthita is a related but separate input.

Brokskat turi and Ushojo taaro star match tārā with final i/o cells and initial stress. Brokskat's rounded root and absent written length differ from Ushojo's long aa; source syllable stress does not settle mora accent.

Brokskat wulo summer matches the upakāla/waalo summer set with a reduced initial sequence and final o. Initial stress is explicit; the exact contraction pathway remains distinct from the separate spring welo token.

Brokskat sari and Ushojo suuri sun match sū́ra/sūrya descendants with final i and initial stress. Ushojo explicitly marks long uu; Brokskat's vowel quality/quantity may require a printed reading, but both are sun, not the adjacent soup etymon13573.

Brokskat picoo tail matches púccha/pic̣oo tail with affricate and final oo stress, independently distinct from lamba/lāṅgūla tails. The long final formation is a potential final-vowel accent class, not a counterexample to unaccented short o adjective endings.

Ushojo ginege take (past) preserves the g/n taking root of gṛbhāyati/giṇ descendants with eg past morphology. Medial stress belongs to this actual verbal formation; root-family only, not a direct old finite accent comparison.

Ushojo ẓugo tall is identical to its long adjective and belongs to dīrghá. Initial stress repeats a single modern lexical item under another gloss, so it must not count as an independent family confirmation.
Ushojo doon teeth matches dánta with nt simplification and loss of final vowel, with a long rounded nucleus. It is a plural gloss but the actual cell is unspecified; no accent is marked.

Brokskat daas and Ushojo dae ten match dáśa with different treatment of the medial sibilant. Ushojo initial stress occurs in an unequal vowel sequence; do not conflate that sequence with a single long aa or infer Brokskat mora from absent marks.

Ushojo si they is the plural member of the sʌ he/she demonstrative paradigm. Its grammatical vowel alternation and lack of accent marking are preserved rather than treated as a distinct lexical etymon.

Brokskat alo proximate they/that matches Shina alo in the āra spatial-demonstrative comparison set. The two records have differing stress marking and grammatical cells; the underlying derivation from āra is provisional and source paradigm evidence is needed.
Ushojo coṛ thief matches cōrá with final vowel loss and rhotic realization. Its short/unlengthened unmarked token supplies no mora outcome.

Brokskat trobes and Ushojo ceiš thirteen preserve the three-plus-ten numeral family with very different contraction. Ushojo initial stress and unequal ei require source sequence interpretation; Brokskat b may be a reading/phonological issue and its stress is unmarked.

Ushojo ana(m)/ani(f) this clearly belongs to the ana demonstrative paradigm. The masculine is explicitly final-stressed; the feminine alternative has no written mark and must be a separate analysis token before accent counting.
Ushojo koṇ thorn matches kaṇṭa through nasal-retroflex cluster reduction and rounded vowel. No accent is marked on the short monosyllable.

Ushojo guṇḍo thread plausibly belongs to guṇá strand with a ḍ/o extension or strengthening. The source marks initial stress, but the extra retroflex stop requires independent formation support; retain provisional status for strict historical comparison.
Brokskat traa and Ushojo ce three match tráyaḥ, with Ushojo tr affrication and final contraction. Neither has marked stress; Brokskat length alone is not an accent outcome.

Brokskat aš and Ushojo aaẓ today match adyá through dy affrication/sibilantization, with different quantity. Their unmarked monosyllables do not settle Palula aáǰ's late accent or the chronology of its lengthening.

Brokskat gip and Ushojo jib tongue match jihvā through contraction and labial stop outcome, with palatal onset spelled g/j. The final voicing difference remains recorded; neither token has a usable accent mark.

Brokskat danii tooth matches dánta with nt simplification and a final ii formation; final syllable stress is explicit. It differs grammatically from unextended doon/daan teeth and belongs in a final-vowel noun class, not a pooled direct old-root preservation count.
Ushojo thoom tree matches stambha post/trunk/tree with cluster simplification and final nasal. The initial aspiration and explicit long oo are segmental evidence; no accent is marked.
